source.title: Ensemble Linear Interpolators: The Role of Ensembling

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted equations have formatting or OCR issues, but the relevant theorem statements and accompanying text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses asymptotic risk analysis for linear least-squares interpolators, rather than the original deep-network experiments, and reports risk behavior as the dimension-to-sample-size ratio changes.
record.gate_note: The paper's own risk and variance results for sketched linear interpolators bear on V4 and part of V6. It does not test deep networks, training epochs, or a fixed-dimension sweep of sample size. Cited results from earlier work are not recorded as rows. Bagged-estimator stability is recorded separately as a finding not covered by a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact asymptotic risk curves for sketched min-norm least-squares interpolators as d/n varies, with finite-sample simulations. For sketched linear regression, this is a new setting. Risk spikes at the shifted threshold γ/θ=1 and falls again beyond it. The spike comes from a diverging variance term. These results bear on V4 (non-deep model class) and V6 (variance-driven peak). The paper's own aim is ensembling stability, so its double-descent evidence is a by-product, not the study's question; hence T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Sketching changes the aspect ratio and shifts the interpolation threshold to γ/θ=1, but risk stays unbounded there because of exploding variance. Bagging reduces that variance (by at least a factor θ), giving bounded risk. It acts as implicit regularization, equivalent to ridge under isotropic features and to a shrunken-covariance model otherwise.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives random-matrix-theoretic risk characterizations for sketched and bagged linear least-squares estimators, rather than experimentally sweeping deep-network size, epochs, or sample size.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpolation threshold depends on the downsampling ratio θ and shifts from γ = 1 to γ/θ = 1. In the underparameterized regime, the sketched estimator's risk depends on the multiplier distribution; in the overparameterized regime, the stated risk is independent of that distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Bagging sketched min-norm interpolators gives bounded limiting risk at the threshold, invariant to the multiplier distribution. It is equivalent to ridge with a fixed implicit penalty λ=(1−θ)(γ/θ−1)∨0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensembling (bagging) linear interpolators acts as implicit ridge regularization and removes the unbounded risk spike at the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Row-subsampling (sketching) shifts the interpolation threshold from d/n=1 to d/(θn)=1 without removing the spike.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak location in linear regression tracks the effective number of retained samples under subsampling.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The results are asymptotic theory in a proportional regime and concern linear least-squares estimators, not deep networks or training-time and sample-size sweeps. The reported figures do not provide uncertainty intervals for finite-sample results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Cited findings from other work were not extracted as study results. Figure-only numerical curves were not transcribed as exact values.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only linear least squares.
No training-time axis; estimators are closed-form min-norm solutions.
Risk is parameterized only by γ=d/n. A fixed-d sample-size sweep is implied by the formulas but never examined or stated.
Only linear least-squares (sketched) estimators; other model classes not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure across size, epochs and samples. The threshold shift to d/(θn)=1 is only an effective-sample-size relabeling within one axis.
No multiple or triple peaks. No test of whether optimally tuned explicit regularization removes the peak.
No reparameterization of complexity to test whether the second descent becomes U-shaped.

missing.what: Finite-sample simulated risks (n=400, 100 repetitions) matching theoretical sketched-estimator curves, with the peak shifting with θ (θ=0.2, 0.6, 1.0) and for multinomial and jackknife multipliers.

Underparameterized risk depends on the multiplier distribution; Bernoulli sketching minimizes it (closed form σ²(γ/θ)/(1−γ/θ)), while multinomial sketching gives a strictly higher risk before the threshold.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: double descent is a by-product here, not the question. The full-sample min-norm curve (Figure 1, Eq. 3.3) is Hastie et al.'s cited result and is rightly not a row. In the isotropic overparameterized formula, risk tends to r² as γ→∞, so the second descent need not fall below the underparameterized minimum. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and peaks near the training-set interpolation size.
Risk as a function of training epochs.
A sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold.
The results concern linear least-squares estimators, not a range of model classes; the paper does not establish the claim across model classes generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across model size, epochs, and sample size.

The study reports variance divergence around the interpolation threshold for sketched interpolators. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: sketched min-norm least square estimator β̂1 (B = 1)
rows.operation_detail: Characterizes asymptotic out-of-sample prediction risk as the dimension-to-sample-size ratio changes.

conditions.value: any distribution satisfying Assumption 3, with downsampling ratio θ

rows.value: For γ/θ < 1: σ²[(1 − γ − γ f(γ))⁻¹ − 1]. For γ/θ > 1: r²(γ/θ − 1)/(γ/θ) + σ²/(γ/θ − 1), with f(γ) defined in Theorem 3.2. The text states that risk explodes as γ/θ approaches 1 from either side.
rows.note: The risk is analyzed as a function of aspect ratio; sketching shifts the threshold to γ/θ = 1. The paper explicitly says the sketched estimator's risk remains unbounded around that threshold.
rows.check: Underparameterized formula is mis-transcribed. The paper's form (Theorem 3.2, Lemma S.4.1) is σ²[γ/(1−γ−f(γ)) − 1], not σ²[(1−γ−γf(γ))⁻¹ − 1]. The overparameterized expression is correct.

rows.subject: sketched min-norm least square estimator β̂1 (B = 1)
rows.operation_detail: Characterizes the asymptotic variance as the dimension-to-sample-size ratio changes.

conditions.value: any distribution satisfying Assumption 3, with downsampling ratio θ

rows.measure: limiting variance component of out-of-sample prediction risk
rows.value: For γ/θ < 1: σ²[(1 − γ − γ f(γ))⁻¹ − 1]. For γ/θ > 1: σ²/(γ/θ − 1). The text states that the risk spike is due to excessive variance.
rows.note: The variance component diverges as the interpolation threshold is approached; the paper identifies this variance escalation as the reason for the risk spike.
rows.check: Same underparameterized transcription error as R1; it should read σ²[γ/(1−γ−f(γ)) − 1]. The bias is 0 for γ/θ<1 and r²(γ/θ−1)/(γ/θ) beyond; only variance diverges, which supports the variance attribution.

rows.subject: bagged min-norm least square estimator β̂B
rows.operation_detail: Characterizes limiting prediction risk as the dimension-to-sample-size ratio changes, with B → ∞.
rows.value: The text states that the limiting risk approaches σ²θ/(1 − θ) from both sides of γ = θ and remains bounded by max{r², σ²θ/(1 − θ)} in both regimes.
rows.note: The authors explain that bagging changes the estimator so it is no longer an interpolator; this bounded-risk result is not itself evidence about the double-descent curve of an individual interpolator.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The bagged estimator is not an interpolator. The paper shows it equals ridge with λ=(1−θ)(γ/θ−1)∨0 (Lemma 3.8), a fixed implicit penalty, not optimally tuned regularization, so it does not test V6's regularization clause.

conditions.value: correlated, with covariance Σ satisfying Assumption 2

rows.value: The text states that the bagged estimator's limiting risk remains bounded, unlike the individual full-sample and sketched min-norm estimators whose risks explode at their interpolation thresholds.
rows.note: This is presented as a stability benefit of bagging; the bagged estimator is not an interpolator.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked; same reasoning as R5 (Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.5).

relationships.condition: Sketched min-norm linear least squares, isotropic and correlated Gaussian-type features, proportional asymptotics (with n=400 simulations)
relationships.reason: Risk is unbounded as γ/θ→1 from either side and decreases again for γ/θ>1. In the isotropic case the risk is r²(γ/θ−1)/(γ/θ)+σ²/(γ/θ−1) (R1, R3). This is a single model class only.
relationships.display_finding: Risk became unbounded as γ/θ approached 1 from either side and decreased again for γ/θ > 1.

relationships.condition: Sketched min-norm linear least squares with noise variance σ²>0
relationships.reason: Bias stays bounded (0 or below r²), while the variance term σ²/(γ/θ−1) (or its correlated analogue) diverges at the threshold. The authors attribute the spike to excessive variance (R2, R4). Only the noise-driven part of V6 is tested.
relationships.display_finding: Bias remained zero or below r², while σ²/(γ/θ−1), or its correlated analogue, diverged at the threshold and generated the spike.
